video_title: Verging on Another Escalation in the Middle East | Ali Vaez
gist: Crisis Group's Ali Vaez argues that eight months into Operation Epic Fury the US-Iran war is a stalemate with escalation risk around the US midterms, as Iran weaponizes selective control of the Strait of Hormuz to squeeze the global economy while a semi-independent Houthi front hits Saudi Arabia. He details severe US interceptor depletion (~70% THAAD, ~50% Patriot), the loss of ~17 regional bases, a US-Israel rift, and a regime in Tehran that is economically battered but politically consolidated. (Public portion only; second hour on Hormuz workarounds and nuclear issue is paywalled.)

themes.theme: US-Iran stalemate and escalation risk around midterms

insights.claim: Eight months into Operation Epic Fury, the US-Iran conflict is in an absolute stalemate, while the Yemen/Houthi front has metastasized and taken on a life independent of US-Iran dynamics.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: De-escalation between Washington and Tehran would not necessarily remove Red Sea shipping risk.
insights.quote: when it gets to Iran and the US, we are in an absolute state of stalemate

insights.claim: At the UN General Assembly in late September, Qatari-mediated talks saw Iran propose reopening the Strait of Hormuz in 7 days instead of the 30 days agreed in the June US-Iran MOU, aiming to tempt Trump with lower energy prices before the midterms.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: A fast-reopening deal exists on the table; any breakthrough could rapidly unwind the oil risk premium.
insights.quote: The Iranians put a proposal on the table that would do so in 7 days.

insights.claim: Washington demanded a nuclear concession be added to any new package because Trump was stung by criticism that the June MOU favored Iran, while Tehran fears extra concessions would signal that pressure works, locking both sides into stalemate.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Both sides' signaling incentives make a near-term deal unlikely, prolonging the Hormuz disruption.
insights.quote: the criticism about the June MOU got under his skin

insights.claim: Washington is betting that a naval blockade, a near air blockade and tougher enforcement of existing sanctions will bring Iran to its knees, an optimism Vaez views as misplaced.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Markets pricing a pressure-driven capitulation by Iran may be too optimistic.

insights.claim: Vaez warns of a meaningful risk of an Iranian 'October surprise' escalation to break the blockade, or a US escalation either before the midterms for a victory or right after when Trump has little to lose.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Event risk around and just after the US midterms is elevated for oil and defense names.
insights.quote: there is a risk that either the Iranians would try to mount an October surprise

insights.claim: Several weeks ago Iran fired a warning-shot anti-ship cruise missile that got through the air defenses of a US warship in the Indian Ocean, signaling what happens if economic pain on Iran becomes too sharp.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Iran has demonstrated credible reach against US naval assets beyond the Gulf, raising shipping and escalation risk.

insights.claim: Vaez is '100%' certain Iran's improved targeting of US naval assets relies on Chinese satellite imagery or Russian intelligence support.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Great-power backing of Iran raises US-China/Russia tension and lengthens the conflict.
insights.quote: Oh, 100%. It's either the Chinese satellites imagery or Russian intelligence

themes.theme: Houthi Red Sea front and Saudi exposure

insights.claim: Recent Houthi missile and drone strikes on Riyadh, including Riyadh's airport with significant casualties including an American, are the worst shock to Saudi Arabia since the 2015-2022 Saudi-Houthi war ceasefire and 2023 Saudi-Iran normalization.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Gulf civilian infrastructure is now in the target set, raising regional risk premia.
insights.quote: especially given how effective the Houthi targeting has been against civilian targets like the Riyadh airport

insights.claim: Trump faces a damned-if-you-do dilemma: breaking the spring US-Houthi ceasefire risks a two-direction threat to US naval assets that benefits Iran, while inaction would be seen as betrayal by the Saudis and erode US credibility.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Whichever way Washington goes, Gulf security costs or US alliance credibility deteriorate.
insights.quote: it's damned if you do and damned if you don't in this case

insights.claim: Air campaigns against the Houthis have failed for 7 years of Saudi-led coalition bombing plus Biden and Trump campaigns, and last spring's 2-month US campaign cost several high-tech fighter jets, so military rollback of the Houthis is not achievable.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Expect the Red Sea threat to persist regardless of US strikes.
insights.quote: it has not worked. And it will not work.

insights.claim: The Houthis are driven by their own agenda (escaping the Saudi port/airport blockade) and are not true Iranian proxies; Iranian sources say Tehran is unhappy the Houthis overextended around Bab el-Mandeb and hit civilian targets.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: A US-Iran deal would not reliably switch off Houthi attacks on shipping.
insights.quote: Iran has, often with the Houthis, it has its foot on the accelerator. It doesn't necessarily have its foot on the brake.

insights.claim: Houthi pressure on Bab el-Mandeb threatens about 5 million barrels of Saudi oil exports to Asia, while Iran-aligned Iraqi militias have attacked Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline that carries 3-5 million barrels to Yanbu to bypass Hormuz, aligning with Iran's goal of keeping energy prices high.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Hormuz bypass routes are themselves under attack, reducing the effectiveness of workarounds and supporting oil prices.
insights.quote: the East-West pipeline which is a pipeline that takes about 3 to 5 million barrels of Saudi oil

themes.theme: Hormuz as economic weapon and global macro fallout

insights.claim: Iran's control of the Strait of Hormuz is the first time a country under great-power economic coercion has been able to squeeze the global economy and every consumer's pocketbook in response, unlike Vietnam, Afghanistan or Iraq.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Energy-chokepoint coercion is a new structural geopolitical risk factor for global inflation.
insights.quote: This is the first time that a country that is subject to economic coercion by great powers is able to squeeze the global economy in response.

insights.claim: Iran never physically closed Hormuz: for the first 2 months it exported its own oil to China with selective passage, using selective attacks to scare off others and spike insurance premiums, and now hits tankers beyond the strait in the Gulf and Sea of Oman.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Insurance premiums and selective-passage dynamics, not a binary closure, drive tanker economics.
insights.quote: They did selective attacks to basically scare off everybody else and jack up insurance premiums

insights.claim: US bombing of Iran's southern shoreline through June-August and contemplation of boots on the ground failed to remove Iran's control over the strait.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Military solutions to reopen Hormuz have been tested and failed; don't price one in.

insights.claim: Vaez calls this the biggest oil shock the world has ever experienced, citing record US Treasury yields, Australia having to issue debt in its own currency, and many countries running out of strategic energy reserves.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Supports a stagflationary macro backdrop with pressure on bonds and energy importers.
insights.quote: this is the biggest oil shock the world has ever experienced

insights.claim: Iran's strategy is a 'never again' moment: make the conflict so costly for the US and the world that Israel's 'mowing the lawn' policy of periodic strikes can never be applied to Iran.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Iran is incentivized to sustain high global energy costs rather than accept a quick ceasefire on Western terms.
insights.quote: This is their never again moment

themes.theme: US military depletion and regional retreat

insights.claim: Expert estimates cited by Vaez put depletion at about 70% of THAAD interceptors, about 50% of Patriot interceptors and about 75% of US long-range missiles, with replenishment taking years rather than months.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Supports multi-year demand for missile defense production and leaves the US exposed to near-term black swans.
insights.quote: about 70% of THAAD missiles have been depleted and around 50% of Patriot missiles

insights.claim: In the medium term the US will fight more asymmetrically, using cheap drones rather than a $100,000 interceptor against a $5,000 drone, and has already copied the Shahed drone design and used it against Iran.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Favors low-cost drone and counter-drone makers over legacy exquisite systems.
insights.quote: It would not use a $100,000 interceptor to shoot down a $5,000 drone.

insights.claim: About 17 US bases across the Gulf, Iraq and Syria were targeted and some are inoperative; Vaez argues rebuilding them makes little sense since they invited attacks rather than deterring them, effectively kicking the US out of the region militarily.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Structural US military retreat from the Gulf changes the security umbrella for Gulf energy assets.
insights.quote: We have about 17 US bases that were targeted.

insights.claim: After an Iranian preemptive strike in Jordan in September killed several Americans, the US is withdrawing assets to Israel, which is becoming a large depot of US military assets.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Concentration of US assets in Israel raises Israel's strategic exposure.

insights.claim: A suspected Iran-linked drone attack on a US base in the UK, mirroring Ukraine's 'spider web' operation against Russia, led the US to withdraw B-1s to the homeland, showing asymmetric tactics spreading across conflicts.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Drone-based asymmetric warfare is diffusing globally, raising base-security and counter-drone spending.

insights.claim: A 'reverse Ukraine' dynamic is emerging: Russia and China, with minimal investment in intelligence, satellite imagery and electronic warfare for Iran, are bogging down the US and draining interceptors that could defend Ukraine or Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: US munitions drain in the Middle East weakens deterrence in Taiwan and Ukraine.
insights.quote: what I call the reverse of the Ukraine phenomenon

insights.claim: Leadership decapitation removed layers of top political and military leaders and replaced them with new figures, making the Iranian system more efficient at bold decisions than under the 86-year-old Khamenei.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Regime-collapse bets are undermined; Iran may act more decisively and less predictably.
insights.quote: it basically made the system much more efficient in making bold decisions

insights.claim: Although 70-80% of Iranians wanted fundamental change before the war, Trump's rhetoric of civilizational erasure redirected anger toward the US and Israel, dashed hopes of outside rescue, and energized the regime's base to rally for nearly 8 months.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: External pressure has strengthened rather than toppled the regime, lengthening the conflict horizon.
insights.quote: the anger that was primarily aimed at the regime is now shared between the regime and the United States and Israel

insights.claim: Iran's economy is horrendous: inflation above 100%, the currency down 50% since the war began, and millions pushed out of work by infrastructure damage such as strikes on steel plants.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Economic pain is severe but the regime transmits it to the population while protecting security forces, so it is not forcing capitulation.
insights.quote: Inflation is above 100%.

themes.theme: US-Israel rift and Israeli war aims

insights.claim: Israel has been sidelined since the April ceasefire because Netanyahu overpromised a regime collapse within days, which is why Trump did not take the Hormuz closure risk seriously, creating a trust deficit in Israeli assessments.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Diverging US-Israel aims reduce coordination and complicate any unified endgame.
insights.quote: Prime Minister Netanyahu overpromised underdelivered

insights.claim: Israel's capacity for attritional war is limited: about 13,000 strikes hit Iran with parts of the country barely feeling the war, while 6 million Israelis went to shelters daily; Iran has not fired on Israel since the end of the 40-day war in April.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Asymmetric home-front costs constrain Israel from re-entering a sustained campaign.

insights.claim: Iran prefers calibrated escalation with the US over reopening the Israel front because Israel, unlike Trump, struck critical economic assets such as steel and petrochemical plants and is seen as unpredictable; during the 40-day war the UAE received more Iranian attacks than Israel, including data centers and Trump Organization-linked firms.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Gulf states, especially the UAE, bear more Iranian targeting risk than Israel, including data center assets.
insights.quote: the UAE for instance received more Iranian attacks than Israel did

insights.claim: Israelis blame the failure to topple Iran on Erdogan, who persuaded Trump to shut down a plan to arm Kurdish minorities for civil war, and believe the concept could be retried; Vaez calls this a misguided oversimplification.
insights.speaker: Ali Vaez
insights.so_what: Israel's belief that further attacks could finish the job sustains risk of renewed escalation.
insights.quote: I think it's an oversimplification and a and a misguided assessment
